title: A little progress I have made so far with my combined arms game. Happy with the way it looks so far.
author: No_Departure7494
selftext: Balancing matches have proven to be very difficult. Artillery, MLRS launcher, SAM missiles, etc. I have to run 100 matches a night (2x the speed while I sleep) to make sure everything is symmetrical and that the player tips the direction of the game.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
AI is terrible at almost all kinds of artwork if you let it build it directly.

Combine AI with procedural techniques, and make the parameters hand-tunable as a final polishing pass, and you will not only get better results, it will also put you fully in control and cut your token budget. You will get artwork that you can "refactor" and that fits into source files that are small enough for GIT.

This is A LOT more work. Is it worth it? That depends on what you compare it to. Compared to learning all the crafts to make all kinds of artwork by hand and then applying those craft to make all your artwork, it will definitely be better use of your time it if it's successful. And you still learn the crafts at a higher, theoretical level on the way.

Also, there are no "one size fits" all tools for this. Making tank meshes and making human meshes are very different processes. That's the beauty of it. You can DIY the specialised tools you need, because code is cheap now. And if you have any knowledge in computer graphics or audio engineering, it definitely helps. If you don't, then you can and will learn on the way while building the tools.

Oh, and AI can reverse-engineer all types of artwork. And it can help you build the tools to reverse-engineer cheaper (like, do a FT of an existing sound and throw it AI to find out how to synthesise it)

comments.author: EnumeratedArray
comments.body:
Running 100 matches a night with AI playing the game probably won't give you the balance you expect.

On paper, it'll be balanced with AI playing against AI. With real players the gameplay will be completely different and your balance gets thrown off.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body:
Yeah that's kind of the idea though. The player is in charge of who wins and who loses, if that makes any sense. Think of it this way.

When one team was overpowered, it was no fun being on that side. They just steamrolled everyone and it felt like none of my decisions mattered. Now winning or losing feels more at the hand of the player.

comments.author: No_Departure7494
comments.body: How? Right now I am focusing on both teams having equal odds of winning and proper CPU optimization so that it can run on any machine?

replies.author: retrorays
replies.body:
sound + ambience is a key part of any game. If you leave this to the end you'll never get something that sounds right. I know from experience. 

how? build the gameplay/graphics. Stop - add sound iterate. go back to gameplay/graphics. With AI the development cycle is short. The \*key\* part of this is when you iterate you identify new ideas, what works and what doesn't. It's like a painter painting... let the mistakes guide you.

replies.author: No_Departure7494
replies.body:
I'm really not sure what your contention is.

I have 2,400 soldiers alone moving on the battle field and am managing to break 60fps most of the time, even with heavy fighting. If the game has massive FPS drops, that's my priority. It will sound good when it runs well.
